Use case examples

Source: vignettes/articles/use-cases.Rmd
use-cases.Rmd
library(parvenu)

parvenu pays off at 100,000 elements or more. There, its functions take milliseconds where base R takes seconds or longer. Looking up 10,000 terms in 100,000 strings takes base R 38s, against 4ms. The examples below are small so they run quickly.

For one call, seconds are often a fine wait. They turn into minutes with dictionaries of thousands of terms, with capture groups or every match from millions of strings, and with tens of millions of times. Where a call repeats, as on every keystroke in a Shiny app or in every bootstrap resample, even a fraction of a second adds up. The README has the numbers.

Coding free text with a keyword table

Free text often has to be sorted into categories: bank transactions into spending categories, free-text medication fields into drugs, open survey answers into codes. A keyword table does this. par_match_term() finds the first keyword each string contains:

transactions <- c(
  "SUPERMART 0412 ZURICH",
  "CITY FUEL STATION 22",
  "Streamflix monthly plan",
  "SUPERMART FUEL 0412",
  "Transfer to savings",
  "Mart & More 17",
  NA
)

keywords <- data.frame(
  keyword = c("supermart fuel", "fuel", "supermart", "streamflix", "mart"),
  category = c("transport", "transport", "groceries", "subscriptions", "groceries")
)

i <- par_match_term(
  transactions,
  keywords$keyword,
  ignore_case = TRUE,
  whole_word = TRUE
)
data.frame(transactions, category = keywords$category[i])
#>              transactions      category
#> 1   SUPERMART 0412 ZURICH     groceries
#> 2    CITY FUEL STATION 22     transport
#> 3 Streamflix monthly plan subscriptions
#> 4     SUPERMART FUEL 0412     transport
#> 5     Transfer to savings          <NA>
#> 6          Mart & More 17     groceries
#> 7                    <NA>          <NA>

Three arguments make this work:

  • Order. The first keyword in the table wins, wherever it occurs in the string. "supermart fuel" comes before "supermart", so the fuel station at the supermarket counts as transport. Put specific keywords before general ones.
  • whole_word = TRUE. Without it, "mart" would match inside "SUPERMART", and a short keyword would turn up inside many longer words. With it, "Mart & More" still matches "mart".
  • ignore_case = TRUE. Statements mix "SUPERMART" and "Supermart". This works in any script, so "é" matches "É".

Rows with no keyword get NA, which shows what the table still misses:

transactions[is.na(i) & !is.na(transactions)]
#> [1] "Transfer to savings"

The same pattern works for:

  • Medication fields. "Aspirin 100mg 1x daily" is matched against a list of drug names, longer names first ("aspirin cardio" before "aspirin").
  • Open survey answers. A codebook of keywords per code, such as "commute" and "traffic" for a transport code.
  • Literature screening. Which drug, gene, or method from a list does each title or abstract name first?
  • Web logs. User agents against a list of bot signatures. These are substrings of longer tokens ("Googlebot/2.1"), so leave whole_word off.

par_match_term() returns one term per string. That suits coding, where each string gets one category. To keep only the strings that contain any term, use !is.na(par_match_term(x, terms)).

Tagging text with every term it names

For tagging rather than coding, par_which_term() finds every term a string contains. It returns their positions in terms, each once:

drugs <- c("aspirin", "ibuprofen", "paracetamol", "codeine")
abstracts <- c(
  "Ibuprofen versus paracetamol for pain after surgery",
  "Aspirin in primary prevention",
  "Physiotherapy for back pain"
)
tags <- par_which_term(abstracts, drugs, ignore_case = TRUE, whole_word = TRUE)
vapply(tags, function(i) paste(drugs[i], collapse = ", "), "")
#> [1] "ibuprofen, paracetamol" "aspirin"                ""

A long table of every pair of string and term is one step away:

data.frame(
  abstract = rep(seq_along(tags), lengths(tags)),
  drug = drugs[unlist(tags)]
)
#>   abstract        drug
#> 1        1   ibuprofen
#> 2        1 paracetamol
#> 3        2     aspirin

Terms that are patterns

Where a term has several spellings or forms, use fixed = FALSE. The terms are then regexes, in the syntax of par_detect(). The earliest term in the list still wins:

tickets <- c(
  "Where is my parcel? Tracking no. 1Z999",
  "I want my money back",
  "Item arrived damaged, please refund",
  "Change my delivery address"
)
topics <- c(
  refund = "refund|money back|reimburs",
  damage = "damaged?|broken",
  shipping = "parcel|deliver(y|ed)|tracking"
)
names(topics)[par_match_term(tickets, topics, ignore_case = TRUE, fixed = FALSE)]
#> [1] "shipping" "refund"   "refund"   "shipping"

All the regexes are searched at once. That is much faster than a search per term, but much slower than literal terms. So list the spellings as literal terms where you can.

Scoring text against a lexicon

Sentiment and topic scores often count how many words from a list each text contains. par_count_term() counts every hit of every term:

reviews <- c(
  "Great food, friendly staff, great value",
  "Cold food and rude staff",
  "Good coffee, bad parking",
  NA
)
positive <- c("great", "friendly", "good")
negative <- c("cold", "rude", "bad")

data.frame(
  reviews,
  positive = par_count_term(reviews, positive, ignore_case = TRUE, whole_word = TRUE),
  negative = par_count_term(reviews, negative, ignore_case = TRUE, whole_word = TRUE)
)
#>                                   reviews positive negative
#> 1 Great food, friendly staff, great value        3        0
#> 2                Cold food and rude staff        0        2
#> 3                Good coffee, bad parking        1        1
#> 4                                    <NA>       NA       NA

Dictionaries such as LIWC list stems, such as "happ*" for "happy" and "happiness". Pass the stems without the * and with whole_word = "start". A term then has to start a word but may end inside one, so "unhappy" doesn’t count:

par_count_term(c("Happy and full of happiness", "Unhappy"), "happ", ignore_case = TRUE, whole_word = "start")
#> [1] 2 0

Hits are counted where they overlap, too. With c("new york", "york"), the string "new york" has two. A term listed twice counts twice, so pass unique(terms) if the list might repeat itself.

Lexicons such as AFINN rate each word from -5 to 5. With weights, par_count_term() sums the rating of every hit, in one pass for all words:

lexicon <- data.frame(word = c("great", "good", "bad", "rude"), score = c(3, 2, -2, -3))
par_count_term(reviews, lexicon$word, ignore_case = TRUE, whole_word = TRUE, weights = lexicon$score)
#> [1]  6 -3  0 NA

Filtering and validating with a regex

par_detect() is grepl() on all cores. It suits large text columns:

log <- c(
  "2026-10-17 12:00:01 INFO request served",
  "2026-10-17 12:00:02 ERROR timeout after 30s",
  "2026-10-17 12:00:03 WARN slow query",
  "2026-10-17 12:00:04 ERROR disk full"
)
log[par_detect(log, " (ERROR|WARN) ")]
#> [1] "2026-10-17 12:00:02 ERROR timeout after 30s"
#> [2] "2026-10-17 12:00:03 WARN slow query"        
#> [3] "2026-10-17 12:00:04 ERROR disk full"

Validating identifiers works the same way. Here, rows whose ID doesn’t have two capital letters followed by six digits:

id <- c("CH123456", "DE654321", "ch123456", "FR12345")
id[!par_detect(id, "^[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{6}$")]
#> [1] "ch123456" "FR12345"

pattern can also have one pattern per string. Here, each ID is checked against the format of its own country:

formats <- c(CH = "^CH[0-9]{6}$", DE = "^DE[0-9]{6}$", FR = "^FR[0-9]{5}$")
country <- c("CH", "DE", "CH", "FR")
par_detect(id, formats[country])
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

Each distinct pattern is compiled once, so a million rows with a few formats cost little more than one pattern.

par_count() counts the matches instead, such as the words in each open survey answer:

answers <- c("Too much traffic on my commute", "ok", "", NA)
par_count(answers, "\\w+")
#> [1]  6  1  0 NA

To find which of many literal terms appear, an alternation such as "aspirin|ibuprofen|paracetamol" is fast in par_detect(). Rust’s regex engine searches all of its branches at once. For a case-insensitive search over many terms, use par_match_term(ignore_case = TRUE) instead, since (?i) makes a large alternation slow.

Factor columns are matched by their levels, so a factor of a million elements with 50 levels costs little more than matching 50 strings. See Performance: fast paths and slow paths for this and other ways to keep calls fast.

Extracting and rewriting parts of strings

par_extract() returns the first match in each string, or NA where there is none. Rust’s regex has no lookaround. To take part of a match, give it a capture group and say which one:

notes <- c("BP 120/80, HR 72", "HR 95", "no vitals", NA)
par_extract(notes, "HR ([0-9]+)", group = 1)
#> [1] "72" "95" NA   NA
as.integer(par_extract(notes, "HR ([0-9]+)", group = 1))
#> [1] 72 95 NA NA

par_replace_all() replaces every match, as gsub() does. In the replacement, $1 stands for the first group, where gsub() takes \\1:

people <- c("Smith, Jane", "Doe, John", "Prince")
par_replace_all(people, "^(\\w+), (\\w+)$", "$2 $1")
#> [1] "Jane Smith" "John Doe"   "Prince"
par_replace_all(c("phone: 044 123 45 67", NA), "[^0-9]", "")
#> [1] "0441234567" NA

par_replace() replaces only the first match, as sub() does. par_extract_all() returns every match, as a list with one character vector per string:

par_replace(c("  padded  ", "x"), "^ +", "")
#> [1] "padded  " "x"
par_extract_all(c("#rstats and #rust", "no tags", NA), "#(\\w+)", group = 1)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "rstats" "rust"  
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> character(0)
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] NA

Only R’s own thread can make R strings, so these run fastest where few strings change, such as redacting the few that hold an email address.

par_locate() finds where the first match is, as a matrix of the first and last character. Use it for substr() or for highlighting:

par_locate(notes, "HR [0-9]+")
#>      start end
#> [1,]    12  16
#> [2,]     1   5
#> [3,]    NA  NA
#> [4,]    NA  NA

Rewriting text with a dictionary

par_replace_term() replaces many literal terms at once, such as spelling variants, abbreviations, or names to redact. It finds them all in one pass. A loop of gsub(fixed = TRUE) would search every string once per term. It could also replace text that an earlier replacement put there:

spelling <- data.frame(
  from = c("colour", "favour", "centre", "NYC"),
  to = c("color", "favor", "center", "New York City")
)
par_replace_term(
  c("Colour and flavour in the centre", "NYC, my favourite"),
  spelling$from,
  spelling$to,
  ignore_case = TRUE,
  whole_word = "start"
)
#> [1] "color and flavour in the center" "New York City, my favorite"

Hits don’t overlap. The leftmost wins. Among terms that start at the same place, the one listed first wins, so list longer terms before their prefixes. With ignore_case = TRUE, the replacement goes in as it is, whatever the case of the hit.

Lookups and joins

par_match() and %par_in% return exactly what match() and %in% return, so they can replace them anywhere. Some common uses:

orders <- data.frame(
  customer = c(101L, 205L, 101L, 999L),
  amount = c(20, 35, 12, 8)
)
customers <- data.frame(
  id = c(101L, 205L, 307L),
  region = c("north", "south", "east")
)

# Bring in a column from another table, as a left join would
orders$region <- customers$region[par_match(orders$customer, customers$id)]
orders
#>   customer amount region
#> 1      101     20  north
#> 2      205     35  south
#> 3      101     12  north
#> 4      999      8   <NA>

# Keep the rows whose key is in a set
orders[orders$customer %par_in% c(101L, 307L), ]
#>   customer amount region
#> 1      101     20  north
#> 3      101     12  north

# Check that every order has a known customer
all(orders$customer %par_in% customers$id)
#> [1] FALSE

Joins often need several key columns, such as a customer and a year. par_match_rows() matches whole rows, without pasting the columns into strings:

orders$year <- c(2025, 2025, 2026, 2026)
targets <- data.frame(
  customer = c(101L, 101L, 205L),
  year = c(2025, 2026, 2025),
  goal = c(500, 400, 300)
)
i <- par_match_rows(orders[c("customer", "year")], targets[c("customer", "year")])
orders$goal <- targets$goal[i]
orders
#>   customer amount region year goal
#> 1      101     20  north 2025  500
#> 2      205     35  south 2025  300
#> 3      101     12  north 2026  400
#> 4      999      8   <NA> 2026   NA

par_match_rows() takes the first match, which suits a lookup table with one row per key. When a key can repeat on both sides, par_match_rows_all() returns every matching pair, as a many-to-many join. Joined with itself, a table returns its groups of equal rows. These may be numeric columns in published data that are copies of each other:

keys <- data.frame(diff1 = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.1), diff2 = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.2))
pairs <- par_match_rows_all(keys, keys)
pairs[pairs$x < pairs$table, ] # each pair of equal rows once
#>   x table
#> 2 1     3

Finding duplicates

par_duplicated() returns what duplicated() returns. Use it to find repeated keys and remove repeated rows. par_unique() returns what unique() returns:

ids <- c("a", "b", "a", "c", "b")
par_duplicated(ids)
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE
par_unique(ids)
#> [1] "a" "b" "c"
sum(!par_duplicated(ids)) # number of distinct IDs
#> [1] 3

# Every row that has a twin, including the first one
visits <- data.frame(
  patient = c(1, 2, 1, 3),
  day = as.Date(c("2026-01-05", "2026-01-05", "2026-01-05", "2026-01-06"))
)
visits[par_duplicated(visits) | par_duplicated(visits, fromLast = TRUE), ]
#>   patient        day
#> 1       1 2026-01-05
#> 3       1 2026-01-05

Binning by sorted breaks

par_find_interval() returns what findInterval() returns: for each value, how many of the sorted breaks are at or below it. That bins values, such as ages into age groups:

age <- c(4, 17, 18, 45, 67, 90, NA)
breaks <- c(0, 18, 65)
groups <- c("child", "adult", "senior")
data.frame(age, group = groups[par_find_interval(age, breaks)])
#>   age  group
#> 1   4  child
#> 2  17  child
#> 3  18  adult
#> 4  45  adult
#> 5  67 senior
#> 6  90 senior
#> 7  NA   <NA>

It also finds which of a set of sorted, non-overlapping ranges each value falls into, such as timestamps into shifts or prices into tax brackets. Give the range starts as vec. With unsorted values, base searches each one from scratch, so the threads help most. 10 million values take tens of milliseconds, where base takes about a second.

Parsing dates and times

Reading dates from text is one of the slowest common steps in base R. A million dates take as.Date() seconds. par_as_date() and par_as_posixct() return what as.Date() and as.POSIXct() return, in milliseconds:

par_as_date(c("2026-01-05", "2026-02-30", NA))
#> [1] "2026-01-05" NA           NA
par_as_date("05.01.2026", format = "%d.%m.%Y")
#> [1] "2026-01-05"
par_as_posixct("2026-01-05 08:30:00.25", tz = "UTC")
#> [1] "2026-01-05 08:30:00 UTC"

Times are parsed in Rust in any time zone. Outside UTC, base R’s own code places the start and end of each day, and every time of a day whose clock changes, which takes longer. Times that span more days than there are times, and uncommon formats, go to base R. ?par_as_date lists the formats that Rust reads.

Ranks, group sums, and interpolation

par_rank() returns what rank() returns. Base rank() is slow where values tie. par_rowsum() sums values by group, as rowsum() does. par_approx() interpolates as approx() does:

scores <- c(ann = 3, bob = 1, cat = 3, dan = NA)
par_rank(scores, ties.method = "min", na.last = "keep")
#> ann bob cat dan 
#>   2   1   2  NA

sales <- c(10, 20, 5, 15)
region <- c("north", "south", "north", "south")
par_rowsum(sales, region)
#>       [,1]
#> north   15
#> south   35

# Temperature at each hour, from readings at irregular times
readings <- data.frame(hour = c(0, 2.5, 6, 9), temp = c(4, 3, 8, 12))
par_approx(readings$hour, readings$temp, xout = 0:9)$y
#>  [1]  4.000000  3.600000  3.200000  3.714286  5.142857  6.571429  8.000000
#>  [8]  9.333333 10.666667 12.000000
